newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Steelmaker Arbed sees steel prices rising.
newsitem.headline: Steelmaker Arbed sees steel prices rising.

text.p: Luxembourg steel maker Arbed said on Wednesday it expected steel prices and demand to increase in 1997 and noted its order books were already showing an encouraging trend.
"Generally speaking, I think from a demand and price point of view the year 1997 will be better than 1996," its president Joseph Kinsch told Reuters in an interview.
"As we already see, the order books are showing a much more positive evolution."

Kinsch said demand and prices in heavy long products had already improved at the end of last year. Since the beginning of this year there was also strong demand for and a positive evolution in the price of flat coated products.

"For the next months it will be possible to proceed to further price increases as demand remains quite strong. We foresee better prices during the rest of the year than we saw at the end of last year or at the beginning of this year."
"I would foresee this improvement from the second quarter onwards - that's not only for heavy long and galvanised products, but also for the other flat products," he said.
In the fourth quarter of 1996 flat product prices mostly remained at the low levels seen in the third quarter, though some galvanised products did already begin to see price rises.
"In flat products...everything is sold already for the first quarter of this year. We are already speaking about the second quarter and there will certainly be a price increase," he said.
Strength in the U.S. and European Union economies would have a positive effect, as would the recent strengthening of the dollar
Kinsch said 1996 had to be considered an unfavourable year, especially compared to 1995 when the first half had been very good.
In October, when Arbed announced a first-half loss of 249 million francs ($7.3 million), he said the second half would be good, but 1996 as a whole would not be a brilliant year.
First trials of Arbed's fourth electric arc furnace are due to take place in May or June this year, with the blast furnace it replaces closing down in the middle of 1997.
"There will be an overlap of about two months. We are within the programme, and there are no foreseeable difficulties," Kinsch said.

When the new furnace at its Esch-Belval site in Luxembourg is operational, Arbed will have completed its transition to the more efficient and adaptable electric steel-making process in its long products sector. A continuous caster is also being built at the complex.
Kinsch said cost benefits of the fourth electric furnace should show through in 1998. ($ = 34.23 Luxembourg Francs)
